quickAnswer: **Hotjar** is the best fit when you need **heatmaps, session recordings, and on-site surveys** to understand why users struggle — not just what they clicked. Skip it if you only need traffic counts or product analytics with feature flags — **Plausible** or **PostHog** cover those roles better.
bestFor: Marketing and UX teams optimizing **landing pages and checkout flows**
Teams asking **why** conversion dropped, not only **where** traffic came from
Organizations running **feedback polls** and surveys on live pages
Complementing GA4 or Plausible with **qualitative behavior** data
notFor: Primary web analytics and channel attribution — pair with GA4 or Plausible
Product analytics with retention cohorts and feature flags — use **PostHog**
Privacy-minimal stacks avoiding session recording — consider policy impact first
Headless or API-only products with no traditional DOM to record

sections.title: Heatmaps & recordings
sections.content:
Hotjar's signature features are **click, move, and scroll heatmaps** plus **session recordings** that replay user journeys. These tools expose rage clicks, form abandonment, and confusing layouts that aggregate metrics miss.

Recordings are sampled based on plan limits — high-traffic sites need higher tiers or filters to stay within quota. Mask sensitive fields in forms and exclude admin areas before going live.

Hotjar complements analytics; it rarely replaces them. Most teams keep a traffic tool and add Hotjar for UX diagnosis.

sections.title: Feedback & surveys
sections.content:
Hotjar includes **Feedback widgets** and **Surveys** to collect on-page qualitative input — useful after redesigns or pricing changes. Targeting rules show prompts on specific URLs or behaviors.

This is valuable for marketing and CX teams without a dedicated research stack. It is not a full user-research repository like Dovetail — export and synthesize insights in your workflow.

Survey fatigue is real; use sparingly on high-intent pages.

sections.title: Privacy & compliance
sections.content:
Session recording captures **DOM content and interactions** — treat Hotjar as processing potentially personal data. Configure **suppression**, honor consent where required, and document processing in your privacy policy.

Hotjar offers GDPR-oriented features and data processing terms, but recording tools generally face **stricter scrutiny** than cookie-light pageview analytics. Legal review before enabling recordings on logged-in areas is prudent.

Not a fit for high-security environments where client-side recording is prohibited.

setupNotes:
**Typical setup:**

1. Create a Hotjar site and install the tracking snippet (often via GTM).
2. Configure **heatmap** and **recording** targets for key URLs.
3. Set up **field suppression** for passwords, payment fields, and PII.
4. Define **surveys or feedback** widgets with targeting rules.
5. Review sample recordings weekly with your UX or growth team.

Expect **1–2 hours** for initial install; ongoing value comes from ritual review, not one-time setup.

**Common pitfalls:** recording internal traffic, unmasked sensitive inputs, and paying for sessions you never watch.
pricingNotes:
Hotjar pricing combines **daily session limits** for recordings and feature access across tiers. Our directory lists entry at **$39/month (Plus)** with higher tiers for more daily sessions and team features — verify current plans on hotjar.com/pricing.

Costs scale with **recorded session volume**, not pageviews alone. Filter recordings to conversion pages to control spend.

Compare total stack cost: Hotjar + Plausible/GA4 vs an all-in-one like PostHog on our [pricing calculator](/calculators/pricing/).
limitations: Not a replacement for web analytics or product analytics baselines.
Session recording has privacy, consent, and performance implications.
High-traffic sites hit daily session caps quickly on lower tiers.
Limited value on non-visual or heavily native app experiences without web UI.
Script weight benchmark pending on AnalyticsVS.

faq.question: Hotjar vs PostHog session replay?
faq.answer: Hotjar optimizes for marketing/UX teams with heatmaps and surveys. PostHog ties replay to product events, flags, and funnels for engineering-led teams.

faq.question: Do I still need Google Analytics with Hotjar?
faq.answer: Usually yes. Hotjar explains behavior on pages; GA4 or Plausible still tells you traffic volume and acquisition channels.

faq.question: Is Hotjar GDPR-compliant?
faq.answer: Hotjar provides compliance tooling, but session recording typically requires consent and careful configuration in EU contexts. Involve legal counsel.

faq.question: Can Hotjar slow my site?
faq.answer: Any third-party script can affect performance. Defer loading, limit recording scope, and test Core Web Vitals after install.
